Qualified Identity, Process, Boundaries, and Infinity
At noon, a cloud hangs above the lake. At 12:05 it has moved, expanded, lost water, gained water, split at one edge, and merged with vapour at another. A child points and says,
“That cloud is getting darker.”
The sentence presupposes that the subject persists through change. Without that presupposition, there is no it to get darker. Yet no sharp boundary tells us which droplets compose the cloud, and no material core remains fixed.
Philosophers use clouds to stage the Problem of the Many. Around the vague object are many overlapping aggregates of droplets, each nearly as good a candidate as the others for being the cloud. If one aggregate is the cloud, what disqualifies its almost-identical neighbours? If many aggregates are clouds, why does perception present one? If the boundary is indeterminate, what happens to ordinary identity claims? The problem is not a linguistic trick, but language helps us glide over it. English supplies a count noun, a singular demonstrative, and the relation same. The grammatical package gives a crisp handle to a diffuse process.
The handle is useful. Human action would stall if every reference required a metaphysical inquiry. But when the same linguistic machinery is carried from clouds to organisms, software, firms, states, and artificial agents, useful compression becomes conceptual debt. The word same answers too many questions at once.
Seven continuities hiding inside one word. Consider seven relations that English routinely calls identity.
Continuity criterion
Explanation
Material continuity
asks whether roughly the same matter persists. A repaired stone wall may remain materially continuous; a flame does not. Even material continuity comes in degrees because matter is lost and replaced
Structural continuity
asks whether the organisation or pattern persists. A whirlpool can maintain a form while water passes through it. A company may preserve its reporting structure while every employee changes
Process continuity
asks whether later stages belong to one uninterrupted activity. A flame persists as combustion, a conversation as reciprocal interaction, and an organism as a network of self-maintaining processes
Causal continuity
asks whether each stage arises through the appropriate causal path from its predecessor. A perfect replica assembled elsewhere may match structurally while lacking the same causal history
Genealogical continuity
asks whether one entity descends from another through copying, reproduction, transformation, or branching. This is central to organisms, texts, software repositories, machine-learning models, and institutions
Role continuity
asks whether a socially defined position persists. “The president,” “the court,” and “the company” may remain the same role-bearing entity despite replacement of persons, rules, and material infrastructure
Informational continuity
asks whether an abstract content is preserved. Two files can instantiate the same bit sequence on different media; two models can implement the same function with different numerical representations; two editions can preserve a text while changing typography
A final variable cuts across all seven: scale. At molecular scale, a body is never the same from moment to moment. At the scale of legal responsibility, it may be continuous for a lifetime. Identity is often not a property simpliciter but a relation indexed to purpose, granularity, and tolerated variation.
English can express every item in this list. The problem is that it normally does not.
“Is this the same model?” invites a binary answer where the real question may be: same(model₁, model₂ | weights, architecture, behaviour, lineage, governance, scale) Without an identity parameter, disagreements can remain invisible. One engineer means identical weights; another means equivalent benchmark behaviour; a regulator means the same accountable system; a user means the service with the same name. All can sincerely answer different questions with the word same.
Things may be stabilised processes. Western metaphysics is often narrated as a conflict between substance and process, with Heraclitus and Whitehead representing processual alternatives to a world of enduring things. The historical picture is more complex, and no natural language maps neatly onto a philosophical doctrine. Still, contemporary philosophy of biology gives a rigorous reason to revisit the noun-centred picture.
In Everything Flows, Nicholson and Dupré argue that living systems are better understood as interdependent processes stabilised at different timescales than as substances that merely undergo change (2018). Metabolism, development, immune regulation, symbiosis, and ecological interaction are not optional activities performed by a pre-existing organism. They partly constitute the organism’s persistence. DiFrisco examines criteria by which biological processes can be identified through variation, and Pradeu develops the idea of genidentity—continuity across a series of states—particularly for cases involving metamorphosis, fusion, or fission.
The process view does not abolish objects. It asks what work object language is doing. A rock may be treated as a relatively slow process; a storm as a fast, open one; an organism as a self-producing network; an institution as a norm-governed pattern maintained through documents, roles, memory, and enforcement. The difference lies partly in characteristic timescale and maintenance regime.
This suggests a replacement for the question “What is X?” when X is dynamic: What must continue happening, at what scale, and within what tolerance, for later stages to count as the continuation of X?
For a cloud, the answer may involve atmospheric dynamics and spatiotemporal continuity. For a river, channel, flow regime, watershed, name, and legal designation compete. For a person, bodily, psychological, narrative, relational, and legal continuities overlap without perfectly coinciding. For a company, control, contracts, brand, assets, organisational memory, and decision procedures matter differently to different observers.
Identity in software and AI. Digital systems reveal the inadequacy of ordinary identity with unusual clarity because copies can be exact while histories diverge.
Suppose model A is copied byte-for-byte to create model B. At the moment of copying, A and B are informationally identical but numerically distinct deployments. If B is fine-tuned, it remains genealogically descended from A but is no longer weight-identical. If A is quantised, architecture and intended function may remain while numerical representation changes. If a serving layer adds retrieval, tools, memory, and policy, users may encounter a system whose behaviour differs substantially despite the same base model. If two companies independently train models that converge on similar behaviour, they may be functionally similar without shared lineage.
Blockchain systems add governance to the puzzle. After a fork, which branch is the original? The answer may depend on state continuity, community recognition, economic weight, protocol rules, name, or normative interpretation. “Original” is not a purely technical property once lineage branches.
The emerging legal and scientific vocabulary of AI will fail if it treats “a model” as a simple object. Audits, licences, safety evaluations, and responsibility need identity criteria. A benchmark result attached to one checkpoint does not automatically transfer to a fine-tuned or tool-augmented descendant. A risk assessment of a service cannot be inherited merely because the marketing name remains stable. The grammar of identity is infrastructure for governance.
The proposed identity operators. Rather than invent unrelated words, SLEnglish can begin with compositional operators: The terms are deliberately plain. Their value lies not in elegance but in preventing a binary predicate from swallowing its parameter. A claim such as
Term
Explanation
matter-same
materially continuous within a stated tolerance
form-same
structurally or organisationally continuous
flow-same
one continuing process
line-same
causally or genealogically continuous
role-same
continuous under a social, institutional, or legal role
info-same
informationally equivalent under a declared representation
effect-same
functionally or behaviourally equivalent for a specified test domain
“The upgraded system is line-same and role-same, but not info-same or effect-same” is immediately more informative than “It is the same system.”
These operators require two additional annotations. Tolerance states how much change is permitted. Scale states the level at which comparison is made. The full form becomes: At the scale of the storm system, two observations may count as the same continuing flow when the interruption is shorter than ten minutes.
or Two models may count as effect-equivalent for diagnostic triage among European adults when their relevant outcome difference remains within a two-percent tolerance.
This may look technical, but ordinary language already embeds hidden parameters.
“The same temperature” means within measurement precision; “the same route” tolerates small deviations; “the same story” tolerates wording changes.
Explicit notation is needed only when hidden tolerances matter.
Gradual identity and the tyranny of binary classification. Some continuities are not yes-or-no. A language, city, ecosystem, or institution can change gradually until the point at which observers cease to treat it as the same. There may be no unique threshold. Binary identity is often a decision imposed for law, record keeping, or action, not a discovered boundary.
A boundary-grade marker would distinguish:
Term
Explanation
sharp boundary
sharp boundary fixed by rule
operational boundary fixed
operational boundary fixed for a purpose
fuzzy boundary
fuzzy boundary with central and peripheral cases
contested boundary
contested boundary with rival criteria
indeterminate boundary where
indeterminate boundary where available facts do not settle membership
The distinction matters for clouds, species, diseases, political movements, markets, and AI capabilities. Calling a model
“autonomous,” a conflict “war,” or an organisation “terrorist” can activate legal and moral regimes.
The world may not provide a sharp natural seam; institutions nevertheless need a rule. A boundary-grade marker would make the imposed character of the rule visible without making action impossible.
Identity as a vector, not a verdict. The strongest proposal of this chapter is that identity should often be represented as a vector of continuities rather than a single verdict. For entities A and B: A comparison between two entities should distinguish material, structural, processual, causal, genealogical, role-based, informational, and functional continuity rather than compressing them into one relation.
Each component can be binary, graded, or unresolved. A legal system may then define which components are decisive for a particular purpose. A biologist, engineer, historian, and regulator may use different projections of the same vector without pretending that one possesses the metaphysically complete answer.
Would such a vocabulary change thought? The hypothesis is testable. Participants could evaluate Ship-of-Theseus cases, corporate transformations, software forks, and biological metamorphoses. One group would use ordinary same; another would learn the identity operators. Researchers could measure consistency, transfer across domains, detection of hidden disagreement, and calibration to stated criteria. The expected benefit is not a single correct metaphysics. It is a lower rate of unnoticed equivocation.
A cloud does not need a passport. But the institutions, models, and collective systems we are building increasingly do. Before issuing one, we should decide what kind of sameness it certifies.
Numbers feel less like words than like features of reality. Three stones remain three stones whether one says three, trois, tres, or nothing. Yet the perceptual world does not deliver exact symbolic number in the form mathematics requires. It offers small quantities that can be recognised rapidly, larger magnitudes that can be estimated, and collections that can be matched one-to-one. A conventional counting system turns these capacities into an indefinitely extendable technology.
This distinction is visible in research with communities whose languages lack extensive exact number vocabularies. Pirahã speakers can compare quantities and perform direct matching, but exact performance declines when objects must be remembered or transformed rather than aligned one-to-one (Gordon 2004; Frank et al. 2008). Mundurukú speakers show sophisticated approximate arithmetic despite a restricted exact number lexicon (Pica et al. 2004). Later work argues that exact concepts are constrained by the range of available count words and practices (Pitt, Gibson, and Piantadosi 2022).
These findings have provoked methodological and interpretive debate, as they should. Language, schooling, notation, material practices, and task familiarity are entangled. The safe conclusion is not that people without a long count list
“cannot think number.”
It is that exact cardinal symbols help preserve and transform quantity across time, memory, and operation. Number words are not mere labels attached to a complete prelinguistic arithmetic. They are parts of a cognitive machine.
When counting conceals the unit. Modern societies count compulsively: users, jobs, papers, deaths, incidents, companies, species, models, and votes. The arithmetic can be exact while the ontology is unstable. What is one active user? One disease case? One AI model? One conflict? One scientific contribution? An exact number attached to an underdefined unit creates the appearance of precision.
Numeral-classifier systems remind us that counting can require a category mediating between numeral and noun. Their conventional classes are not solutions to contemporary measurement, but the grammatical principle is powerful: one must state what kind of one is being counted.
A designed count classifier could mark the unit principle:
Term
Explanation
Bounded physical object
a unit individuated primarily by a physical boundary
Individuated event
a unit defined as one occurrence under an event-counting rule
Continuing process
a unit defined by the persistence of an organised dynamic rather than fixed matter
Legal unit
an entity whose countable identity is fixed by law, contract, or registry
Lineage unit
a genealogical continuation that may survive copies, branches, or versions
Deployment unit
one operationally instantiated system in a particular environment
Statistical cluster
a grouping whose unity depends on a stated method and parameterisation
Thus
“twenty models” becomes “twenty deployments of four lineages” or “twenty weight files from one architecture.”
The number becomes more complex and more honest.
Zero and the invention of absence. Zero is often described as a discovery, an invention, or both. The physical world contains empty containers and missing expected objects, but the mathematical zero is not identical to any particular absence. It functions as a number, a placeholder, an identity element, a coordinate, and a boundary between signs. Stable notation allowed absence to participate in calculation.
Ordinary English still handles absence badly.
“There is no evidence” can mean that nobody looked, that a search found nothing, that available methods cannot detect it, that evidence once existed but was lost, or that the hypothesis predicts no observable trace.
“The feature is absent” may mean nonexistence, non-detection, deactivation, irrelevance, or failure of a classification rule.
We need at least four negative states:
Term
Explanation
empty
a defined container has zero members
missing
an expected item is not present
undetected
a search did not find an item within known sensitivity
nonexistent-under-model
the operative ontology contains no such item
A fifth, uninstantiated, applies to a possible type with no current token. A sixth, inapplicable, says that the question itself does not fit the object. Databases often collapse all six into null. Natural language often does the same.
The several infinities hidden in infinity. The word infinite performs even more work than same. It can mean that a process has no last step, that a set is treated as a completed totality, that a magnitude is unbounded, that a series diverges, that a mathematical object has transfinite cardinality, that resolution continues without practical limit, or merely that something is unimaginably large.
The historical distinction between potential infinity and actual infinity remains useful. Potential infinity characterises a process that can always be continued: for every number, another can be produced. Actual infinity treats an infinite collection or structure as complete enough to quantify over mathematically. Modern set theory formalises actual infinite sets; Cantor’s work distinguishes different infinite cardinalities. Analysis uses limits to reason rigorously about unbounded processes and arbitrarily fine variation.
The claim that infinity has “no counterpart anywhere in the real world” is too strong. Whether physical space, time, divisibility, field values, or the cosmos instantiate any form of actual infinity is a live question in physics and metaphysics. Some theories contain infinities; some physicists treat singularities as signs of theoretical breakdown; cosmological observations do not settle whether the universe is spatially finite. The responsible claim is narrower: human beings do not encounter a completed infinite collection through ordinary perception, yet formal infinity has transformed mathematics, theology, cosmology, economics, and culture. The Stanford Encyclopedia’s recent survey rightly treats mathematical, physical, cosmological, and theological infinity as related but distinct problems (Easwaran et al. 2025).
A better ordinary vocabulary should separate:
Term
Explanation
endless
no terminal stage is specified
unbounded
no finite upper bound exists in the model
divergent
a sequence or process fails to converge in a specified way
actual-infinite
a completed mathematical totality governed by an axiom system
transfinite
belonging to formal orders of infinite size
practically inexhaustible
finite or unknown in extent but impossible to enumerate with available resources
outfinit
open-ended beyond every current operational boundary while every realised stage remains finite
The last term is a deliberate conceptual invention. Outfinit is not a substitute for mathematical infinity. It names systems whose continuation has no relevant designed endpoint, although every physical or computational realisation is bounded. An expanding research programme, evolutionary process, generative search, or indefinitely extensible proof practice can be outfinit without containing a completed infinite object. The term protects us from two errors: treating the unfinishable as literally infinite, and treating finite implementation as evidence of a final conceptual limit.
Infinity as cultural operator. Infinity does not remain inside mathematics. Religions use it for divine attributes and eternity. Economics invokes indefinite growth. Technology markets “unlimited” storage or scale while relying on finite infrastructures. Political narratives imagine permanent institutions and inexhaustible progress. Personal identity is sometimes invested in digital traces expected to persist without horizon.
These transfers are rarely innocent. A model that assumes infinite substitutability of resources can erase ecological thresholds. A cultural image of endless growth makes saturation or sufficiency appear as failure. Conversely, an overreaction against infinity can cripple abstraction: calculus, probability, topology, and modern physics rely on disciplined idealisation.
The relevant distinction is between formal permission and ontological commitment. One may quantify over infinite structures inside a mathematical theory without claiming that the universe contains a corresponding completed object. One may use an infinite-horizon optimisation while recognising that institutions and agents are finite. A grammar for infinity should mark the mode: The vocabulary should distinguish formal infinity, infinity as a physical hypothesis, procedural endlessness, and operational outfinity.
Much philosophical confusion occurs when a property moves silently from one mode to another.
Negative, imaginary, and probabilistic objects. Negative numbers once appeared less natural than positive counts; imaginary numbers carried their scepticism in their name. Their power came from rules of operation and integration into systems, not from resemblance to visible objects. Probability similarly converts uncertainty into quantities that can be combined, updated, scored, and compared—imperfectly, but far beyond vague confidence words.
These cases support the book’s constructive thesis. A useful concept need not correspond to a simple object. It must provide stable distinctions, compositional operations, inferential discipline, and practical gain. The goal for collective agency or identity is not to find a hidden
“thing” matching the term.
It is to create representations that support better reasoning.
The analogy has limits. Mathematical symbols work in highly controlled systems; social and metaphysical concepts are open-textured and norm-laden. A responsibility vector cannot attain the universality of arithmetic. But it can still outperform a single vague noun, just as a multidimensional medical profile can improve on the binary
“healthy/sick” without becoming pure mathematics.
What else is hidden by exactness. Modern metrics often combine exact numbers with uncertain constructs. A university ranks seventh; a model scores 91.3; a country has a freedom score of 78; a worker has a productivity index. The precision belongs to the calculation, not necessarily to the concept. Goodhart’s law captures one failure mode: when a measure becomes a target, optimisation can detach it from the underlying goal.
A metric-mode marker should therefore distinguish measurement, proxy, target, and constitutive rule. Temperature is measured; citation count is a proxy for influence; a benchmark becomes a target when developers optimise against it; a legal threshold can constitute eligibility rather than merely detect it. The same number behaves differently in each mode.
Counting is among humanity’s greatest cognitive achievements. Its next refinement may be learning when the unit, boundary, and mode of infinity are doing more philosophical work than the numeral.

claims.statement: The proposed controlled layer is called SOP Lang English, or SLEnglish. Its statements use a regular outer form with named parameters. Each statement receives an explicit identity that later statements can reference. A path selects an operator whose contract defines its meaning. This arrangement concentrates semantic variation in libraries instead of an expanding parser grammar. The book explains the syntax alongside its costs and provisional design choices. You can read it as an inspectable proposal rather than a finished universal language.
qualifiers: An introduction to the book’s argument; proposed architectures remain proposals, and medical or market metaphors are not advice.

spans.quote:
Design Objectives and the Uniform Sentence Form
SLEnglish, short for SOP Lang English, is the controlled executable layer proposed here. It receives task-relevant interpretations of natural language and represents them through a uniform statement form, explicit SSA identities, path-addressed verbs, named parameters, typed values, contexts, and references. The design concentrates semantic variation in operator contracts so that parsing, validation, diffing, provenance, and execution can use a stable outer grammar.
The design starts from a practical observation. When language models translate prose into JSON, triples, code, graphs, or solver formulas, each target recreates a different surface convention for entities, relations, claims, evidence, variables, contexts, and questions. This proliferation makes semantic comparison difficult. SLEnglish introduces one regular outer envelope while leaving the operator libraries and interpretation profiles open. The intended gain is not expressive novelty alone; it is stable identity, explicit roles, source alignment, canonical diffing, and portable validation across heterogeneous methods.
The canonical form is deliberately visible before its details are elaborated: `@ssa-id x/y/name.sle parameter-name value parameter-name value ... .` The token beginning with `@` creates a new Single Static Assignment identity. The following path selects a versioned operator contract. The remaining tokens form named parameter–value pairs. The final period is a separate terminator. An operator path may contain any number of directory levels. `knowledge/evidence/report.sle`, `language/english/aspect/progressive.sle`, and `science/clinical/trial/adverse-event.sle` are all valid structural shapes when their files and dependencies are declared.
The folder path is not decorative punctuation. It is the namespace. A repository can place related operator files under nested directories, and ordinary file-system tools can browse, version, hash, review, package, and distribute them. A project may organise a local operator at `projects/climate/region-a/ice-loss.sle`; a shared standard may expose `knowledge/causation/structural.sle`; a language-specific library may contain `language/quechuan/evidential/reported.sle`. No global rule limits the depth. The root manifest and import lock determine which paths are visible and which version each path denotes.
A slash-separated operator path follows the structure of the package folders. A verb can therefore be addressed at arbitrary depth, for example `knowledge/evidence/report.sle`, `science/measurement/observe.sle`, or `social/agency/collective/decide.sle`. The path provides an intuitive namespace, supports ordinary version-control tooling, and allows independent libraries to grow without imposing a fixed number of namespace levels.
The uniform sentence form is stricter than most controlled natural languages. It does not preserve subject–verb–object grammar, articles, agreement, conjugation, passive alternations, or free attachment. English remains present in operator names, parameter names, labels, and reversible renderings. The execution syntax is closer to a semantic assembly language. This is acceptable because an LLM or another semantic parser performs most initial translation. The human task is review and correction rather than unaided composition of every line.
Strictness is useful only when it targets the right layer. The parser should remain small: it recognises bindings, paths, atomic values, quoted values, references, parameter names, and the final period. It should not contain a universal grammar of science or encode evidentiality, causation, identity, and social authority as special productions. Those distinctions belong to operator contracts stored in `.sle` files. Extension therefore adds semantic libraries without repeatedly changing the parser.
A SLEnglish operator is called a verb because it constructs or transforms a semantic object, not because it must correspond to an English lexical verb. `knowledge/evidence/report.sle` links a proposition to a report. `language/reference/inclusive-we.sle` constructs a participant relation. `knowledge/identity/process.sle` qualifies continuity. `social/collective/decide.sle` represents an authorised or otherwise specified collective decision. `execution/query/why.sle` asks for a derivation, provenance chain, causal path, or assumption record. The operator owns the legal parameter names and the semantic contract associated with its output.
The language distinguishes a value from the node that produced or states it. `$name` requests the primary value associated with an earlier SSA identity and creates an explicit data dependency. `~name` refers to the node itself, including its semantic identity, provenance, status, alternatives, and source alignment. A measurement value may be compared through `$measurement`; the measurement statement may be cited through `~measurement`. This separation prevents a common error in which a proposition, its numerical result, and its evidence record are treated as interchangeable.
Single assignment preserves history. A node is created once within a source revision and is never mutated in place. A correction creates a successor node or a new execution epoch, linked by supersession or derivation. This makes it possible to explain why an earlier conclusion was accepted, identify which downstream results depend on a revised premise, and compare two interpretations without erasing either one. SSA is therefore not merely a compiler convention. It is part of the provenance and semantic-diff model.
The canonical source is intentionally verbose where explicitness reduces error. Parameter order is not used to infer semantic roles. A transfer states agent, theme, recipient, origin, destination, time, and context through names when the active contract requires them. A profile can require source, valid time, unit, uncertainty, or identity mode for particular classes of statement. Editors may present compact forms, but the canonical representation does not rely on a hidden default that changes across tools.
The decision to expose all semantic constructions as operators is broader than the initial core proposal. Ordinary English constructions and cross-linguistically attested categories can enter the same library system. Progressive aspect, reportative evidence, switch-reference, logophoric perspective, alienable possession, collective agency, structural causation, process identity, and threshold effects differ in content but not in the outer mechanism by which they become inspectable and executable. The appendices provide a candidate inventory rather than a fixed final standard.
Element
Meaning in canonical SLEnglish
`@ssa-id`
Creates one stable node identity in the current source revision. The identity is assigned once and can be referenced by downstream statements.
`x/y/name.sle`
Selects a path-addressed operator contract. The path may contain arbitrary directory depth and is resolved through manifests, imports, versions, and content digests.
`parameter-name value`
Supplies a typed role to the selected operator. The contract declares required, optional, repeated, and mutually constrained parameters.
`$name`
Dereferences the primary semantic value produced by a previous node and establishes a value dependency.
`~name`
Passes a reference to the semantic node, preserving proposition identity, provenance, status, alternatives, and source links.
Quoted literal
Preserves textual content including spaces. Its datatype, language, or source role is supplied by the operator contract or an explicit parameter.
Atomic symbol
Names a declared entity, type, unit, enum member, context, model, or other symbol without natural-language inflection.
Final period
Terminates the statement. It is separated by whitespace from the final value, so the `.sle` extension remains unambiguous.
@core slenglish/core/import.sle module
"slenglish-core" version "0.3" root "slenglish".
@alice slenglish/core/entity.sle type person label
"Alice".
@sample slenglish/core/entity.sle type biological-sample label
"Sample A".
@transfer language/event/transfer.sle agent $alice theme $sample origin freezer-1 destination lab-2 time
"2026-08-22T09:00Z".
@reported knowledge/evidence/report.sle proposition ~transfer source lab-log source-depth 1 confidence 0.98 .
@accepted slenglish/core/assert.sle proposition ~transfer context actual-world .
The example illustrates the division between proposition construction and commitment. The transfer node states a semantic event. The report node records an evidential relation to that event. The assertion node accepts the event in a named context. Another context may retain only the reported claim without accepting its content. This separation permits testimony, belief, quotation, hypothesis, denial, and assertion to share one proposition without collapsing their epistemic status.
Canonicalisation is required for reproducible tooling. Whitespace, numeric representation, booleans, parameter order, path resolution, aliases, repeated parameters, strings, and missing-value atoms receive deterministic serialisations. Two source views that resolve to the same operator identity and parameter structure should produce the same canonical node when their meaning under the selected contract is the same. Canonical equality does not imply metaphysical equivalence; it means identity within the declared representation.
The syntax remains a proposal subject to evidence. The final period might prove unnecessary, the `$` and `~` distinction might require clearer notation, one file per operator may be too granular, or path-addressed names may need a registry alias for portability. These choices should be tested against parser complexity, translation accuracy, correction time, semantic diff quality, repository maintenance, and user comprehension. Their provisional status is part of the specification rather than a weakness to conceal.

Files, Operator Contracts, Parameters, Contexts, Rules, and Queries
The semantic library is the substantive part of SLEnglish. A path becomes executable only when its file declares a contract. The contract specifies the operator’s output kind, required and optional parameters, accepted value types, cardinalities, determinism, purity, monotonicity, context behaviour, effect class, compatible interpreter profiles, canonical parameter order, inverse rendering guidance, validation cases, and version history. A directory of names without these properties is a vocabulary; it is not an executable language library.
Operator files can be organised at any useful depth. A root manifest declares package identity, dependencies, version constraints, content digests, exported roots, default labels, and conformance expectations. A directory may contain a shared role registry, type declarations, examples, tests, lowering adapters, and migration rules. The visible path remains intuitive because the folder layout corresponds to conceptual scope. The compiled identity remains stronger because it includes the package digest and resolved version.
The path tree should not be mistaken for a single taxonomic truth. Different communities may publish competing causal, social, clinical, or linguistic libraries. A project can import both under distinct roots, declare bridge mappings, and record where the mappings are partial. The standard concerns resolution, typing, provenance, and comparison. It does not require every discipline to agree on one ontology before executable work can begin.
Parameters provide semantic roles shared across operators. claims.statement: A language model can propose the translation into this controlled layer. The proposal must preserve source spans, unresolved references, alternatives, and introduced assumptions. Deterministic checks then inspect structure, types, contexts, and required provenance. Passing those checks still does not establish that the translation means what the source meant. LLM Translation, Deterministic Validation, and Auditable Meaning
The principal advantage of using a language model at the front end is economic. A rigid target language no longer needs to anticipate every surface form through hand-written parsing rules. The model can propose entities, events, relations, scopes, evidence links, and candidate operator paths from unrestricted prose. The principal danger is equally clear: the model can introduce precision that the source did not contain. SLEnglish therefore treats model output as a candidate compilation, not as accepted meaning.
A translation request includes the source revision, active operator libraries, type environment, task contract, desired interpretation profile, and examples of valid canonical source. The model returns SLEnglish candidates together with source-span mappings, unresolved references, alternative readings, introduced assumptions, unsupported constructions, and a translation confidence that is explicitly not a truth probability. The output must parse without an automatic repair stage that silently changes semantics. A failed parse is a visible compiler failure.
The deterministic parser performs only lexical and structural work. It recognises SSA identities, operator paths, parameter–value pairs, strings, numbers, booleans, declared missing-value atoms, `$` references, `~` references, and statement boundaries. It does not infer an omitted parameter, select an ontology, or reinterpret a malformed line. The resolver then binds every path to a locked operator contract. The schema validator checks parameter legality and cardinality. The type checker checks values and references. The context checker checks world and profile compatibility. The provenance checker confirms required source links.
Validation cannot establish semantic fidelity by itself. A syntactically valid representation may still misread the source. The toolchain therefore needs contrastive and round-trip tests. A controlled renderer produces a plain-language account from the candidate without consulting the original wording. Reviewers compare the material commitments. Paraphrase tests compile meaning-preserving variants and compare canonical structures. Semantic mutation tests alter negation, quantifier scope, participant order, source mode, time, exception, or modality and check that the appropriate node changes while unrelated nodes remain stable.
Ambiguity is represented rather than solved invisibly. When a phrase permits two consequence-relevant attachments, reference assignments, scopes, or causal readings, the compiler creates alternatives under an interpretation set. A model can rank them, and a user can select or reject them, but ranking alone does not authorise collapse. A downstream query may return a conclusion that holds under every represented alternative, one that holds under at least one, one that holds under none, or an unknown status because the set is incomplete.
Grounding is layered. Lexical grounding proposes operator paths and symbols. Referential grounding links mentions to entities or preserves distinct candidates. Ontological grounding selects types and relations. Temporal grounding locates states and events. Evidential grounding connects propositions to observations, reports, data, or assumptions. Normative grounding identifies issuer, mandate, jurisdiction, and effective time. Each layer produces its own diagnostics so that a source mismatch is not reported generically as a reasoning failure.
Coverage is part of negative reasoning. Failure to retrieve a prior publication does not establish that none exists; absence of a row in an open dataset does not establish non-existence; a bounded email export does not establish that no message was sent outside the export. A coverage object records the source set, revision, retrieval method, exclusions, temporal interval, schema, and closure policy. A query that requests absence or completeness must cite a compatible coverage object or return a weaker status.
Identity compilation requires special restraint. Repeated labels, titles, aliases, versions, and descriptions are not merged solely by string similarity. Candidate identity links name their criterion and evidence. Strict identity licenses substitution only under a declared profile. Process continuity, lineage, material overlap, legal continuity, and functional equivalence remain separate relations. A translator that cannot determine the intended relation should preserve alternatives or emit an unresolved identity obligation.
The trusted computing base should be small relative to the overall system. It includes canonical source handling, path and version resolution, schema validation, type checking, profile selection, verified or well-tested lowering components, interpreter receipts, result-envelope validation, and source-linked diagnostics. Models, retrieval systems, heuristic ontology matchers, approximate memories, and prose renderers remain outside that boundary. They can propose useful work without being allowed to redefine accepted semantics silently.
Human review is not a single approval button. A domain expert may judge whether a measurement or causal concept is appropriate. A source specialist may verify a quotation and reference. A methodologist may review a statistical or formal lowering. An authorised institutional actor may approve an operational effect. The representation records who accepted which commitment under which role. This permits selective responsibility rather than asking one reviewer to certify the entire artefact.
Correction must be local. When a reviewer changes an evidence mode, reference link, boundary, unit, or operator path, the compiler creates a revised node and preserves unaffected identities. The dependency graph identifies which validations, derivations, queries, and rendered claims require reconsideration. Full recompilation remains available as a reference, but local invalidation makes long-lived scientific objects economically maintainable.
The final renderer is constrained by a claim-licensing relation. It receives accepted result objects, proof or evidence links, contexts, conditions, and unresolved limitations. It may choose wording and explanatory order, but it may not turn possibility into actuality, conditional support into unconditional fact, conflict into consensus, or a report into direct observation. Each generated sentence maps back to the nodes that license it. This does not make generated prose infallible; it makes overstatement detectable.
The complete translation record should retain the source span, candidate generation metadata, active libraries, model identifier, prompt or instruction digest, alternatives, deterministic diagnostics, reviewer changes, and final accepted nodes. Privacy and intellectual-property constraints may limit what can be stored, but the limits themselves should be recorded. A published semantic artefact that omits its translation history may remain useful, yet it offers a weaker basis for audit and reproducibility.
The research question is whether this intermediate step improves outcomes over simpler alternatives. Direct prompting may be sufficient for low-consequence summarisation. A JSON schema may be sufficient for extraction. A conventional compiler may be superior in a narrow language. SLEnglish earns its cost only where reusable semantic libraries, cross-task queries, explicit alternatives, provenance, and local correction provide measurable value.

Does the source conform to the one-shape syntax without silent repair?
Path resolution
Does every operator path resolve to a locked and versioned contract?
Schema
Are required parameters present and are illegal or repeated parameters rejected?
Type
Do values, node references, and returned objects satisfy declared types and cardinalities?
Context
Are worlds, jurisdictions, scenarios, and interpretation profiles combined only through declared bridges?
Grounding
Can every accepted symbol and semantic commitment be traced to source material, data, a definition, or an explicit assumption?

Are negative and completeness claims licensed by the examined domain and closure policy?

Do round-trip, contrastive, paraphrase, mutation, and human review tests support the source-to-node mapping?

Did the selected interpreter apply the named semantics, bounds, versions, and assumptions?

Does every sentence in the final explanation remain within the accepted result envelope?

claims.statement: SLEnglish is not tied to one mandatory reasoning engine or circuit runtime. Different compatible fragments may use rules, databases, solvers, simulations, or generated code. Each adapter must declare what it preserves, rejects, or approximates. A statistical estimate must not become indistinguishable from a deductive proof. The comparison chapters acknowledge what established standards and controlled languages already provide. The proposed layer must earn its place beside those existing capabilities. Reading those comparisons helps separate a useful interface from an unnecessary extra language.
qualifiers: An introduction to the book’s argument; proposed architectures remain proposals, and medical or market metaphors are not advice.

spans.quote:
Interpreter Families, Generated Code, and Circuit Runtimes
SLEnglish is designed to be interpreted, but it is not defined by one interpreter. The surface representation provides typed operators, values, references, contexts, rules, queries, and dependencies. A backend adapter may lower a compatible fragment to Datalog, Answer Set Programming, a description-logic reasoner, SPARQL, SQL, an SMT or CSP solver, a temporal engine, a theorem prover, a simulation framework, conventional generated code, or another domain method. The adapter must state which semantics it preserves and which constructs it rejects or approximates.
Backend neutrality is not the absence of semantics. Every operator contract names compatible profiles and expected outputs. A relational closure operator may have a Datalog interpretation. A defeasible rule may require an ASP profile. A quantity constraint may lower to SMT with units normalised beforehand. A temporal process may use interval algebra, event calculus, automata, or model checking. A statistical claim may invoke an analysis package whose result is evidence rather than logical entailment. The common result envelope records status, context, assumptions, bounds, provenance, and an engine-specific receipt.
Generated conventional code is a legitimate interpretation route. An operator family may compile into a typed host-language library, a database query plan, a workflow definition, a test suite, or a simulation configuration. Generated code must remain subordinate to the semantic source: versions, inputs, environment, side effects, outputs, and validation tests are recorded. The existence of code does not prove that the generated procedure faithfully represents the source; the compiler contract and tests address that question.
Dynamic SOP Lang circuits provide one execution substrate for SLEnglish. The circuit research programme studies typed nodes, explicit dependencies, composable structures, bounded execution, provenance-bearing connections, validation, and interpreter composition (ScriptaHub 2026). These properties align naturally with SLEnglish because SSA identities and named references already expose dependency structure. Circuit execution can therefore be evaluated alongside rule engines, graph stores, solvers, temporal systems, generated code, and domain-specific interpreters.
A source-language boundary allows execution technologies to evolve independently. Circuit schedulers, activation rules, memory systems, dynamic expansion, and resource control can change behind an adapter while SLEnglish operator contracts remain stable. The same SLEnglish package can also target a different runtime when its contracts map more directly to another formalism. Backend comparisons can therefore measure correctness, performance, interoperability, and review cost while holding the source representation constant.
A circuit backend gives operational meaning to SLEnglish dependencies. `$` references can become dataflow edges; `~` references can become proposition or provenance edges; imports can become module dependencies; rules and queries can generate demand; node hashes can support caching; declared purity and monotonicity can support incremental or reordered evaluation. These mappings define an adapter contract and can be tested without fixing one scheduler or memory architecture in the language specification.
Other backends may interpret the same structure differently. A graph database can store nodes and indexed roles without treating them as scheduled computation. A Datalog compiler can materialise compatible relations and recursive rules. An SMT compiler can generate variables and constraints for a bounded query. A theorem-prover adapter can generate declarations and proof obligations. A code generator can map operators to host-language calls. A hybrid runtime can route different subgraphs to specialised methods while retaining one evidence and dependency record.
Heterogeneity requires explicit conversion. Moving from a probabilistic estimate to a Boolean threshold, from an OWL class assertion to a closed-world database fact, or from an approximate retrieval score to an accepted premise changes guarantees. Conversion operators should appear in the graph and state information loss, threshold, calibration, and authority. A common envelope must not disguise incompatible semantics as if every node participated in one uniform proof system.
Effects require a separate authorisation layer. A SLEnglish proposition may describe, recommend, require, or hypothesise an action without causing the action to occur. An operational request can be interpreted only by a runtime with the relevant capability, policy, identity, budget, privacy permission, and approval. This prevents a sentence such as ‘the sample should be heated’ from becoming a laboratory command merely because it has a syntactically valid representation.
Execution should be epoch-based. An epoch binds the source revision, operator locks, compiler versions, active contexts, selected profiles, interpreter versions, policies, and captured external inputs. A later epoch can reuse a cached result only when the operator contracts and invalidation rules justify reuse. Full replay remains the reference for validating incremental execution. Historical results retain the environment and assumptions under which they were produced.
A backend must be able to stop with a structured status. Unsupported operator, unresolved type, incomplete coverage, ambiguous grounding, unavailable engine, resource exhaustion, policy denial, inconsistent assumptions, and failed certificate are distinct outcomes. Returning unknown with a reason is preferable to asking an LLM to improvise across an unsupported gap. The result envelope can distinguish entailed, refuted, possible, necessary, conflicted, unsupported, bounded, timed out, and unknown without pretending that all statuses arise from the same logic.
Approximate retrieval and high-dimensional representations may assist operator selection or source discovery, but they do not define accepted consequence. Similarity can nominate a candidate path, related passage, or possible analogy. The candidate returns to the typed and source-grounded pipeline. If lexical search, graph indexes, embeddings, vector-symbolic methods, or a language model are used, the system should compare recall, semantic precision, latency, memory, provenance quality, and downstream false assurance. The language itself remains independent of the winning retrieval method.
The engine router should be driven primarily by declared contracts. An LLM can propose a plan, but a deterministic registry should check that every operator supports the selected lowering and that the requested guarantee is available. The router records why a backend was selected, what fragments were not handled, what conversions occurred, and which certificates or test results were returned. An unsupported request remains an explicit obligation rather than being silently delegated to free-form generation.
Scientific work combines exact proof, statistical estimation, simulation, measurement, causal modelling, database retrieval, interpretation, and institutional judgement. SLEnglish represents their common semantic dependencies while preserving the boundaries among their execution semantics. A result therefore records the operator contracts, conversions, assumptions, evidence, and backend receipts that license it.
The same representation supports several levels of execution. It can serve as a typed annotation format, semantic diff layer, compilation target for domain tools, query-oriented research object, or interchange representation between LLMs and existing systems. Where a general runtime is useful, the dependency graph can coordinate multiple interpreters. This makes runtime choice an empirical engineering variable rather than a property encoded into the source grammar.
The backend-agnostic position is therefore an empirical commitment to modularity. It can be falsified. If most operators require backend-specific surface syntax, a common source may become an unhelpful abstraction. If adapters introduce unacceptable semantic loss, direct authoring in established formalisms may be better. If the dependency structure adds little to correction or reuse, a simpler frame representation may suffice. The programme should preserve the evidence required to reach any of these conclusions.
Interpreter family
Appropriate SLEnglish contribution and required caution
Datalog or deductive database
Supports typed facts, recursive closure, and explainable rules; requires explicit treatment of negation, stratification, and closure.
Answer Set Programming
Supports defaults, exceptions, competing models, and optimisation; result semantics and priorities must be named.
RDF, SPARQL, and graph systems
Support graph interchange, federation, and query; n-ary events, context, and profile assumptions require explicit modelling.
Description logic or OWL
Supports class and property reasoning within decidable profiles; it should receive only compatible fragments.
SMT, CSP, SAT, and optimisation
Support arithmetic, finite-domain, scheduling, and constraint obligations; units, bounds, and encoding correctness must be recorded.
Temporal engine or model checker
Supports event ordering, persistence, state transitions, and temporal properties; the chosen time and transition semantics must be explicit.
Theorem prover or proof assistant
Supports deductive proof under formal definitions; fidelity of the formalised statement remains a separate obligation.
Generated conventional code
Supports procedures, simulations, tests, and integrations; environment, effects, versions, and semantic tests remain part of the record.
Dynamic SOP Lang circuit runtime
May exploit typed dependencies, bounded execution, caching, and provenance; it is an optional substrate described in a separate research programme.
Human or institutional interpreter
Remains necessary for contested meaning, legitimacy, ethical authority, and domain judgement; the role and decision must be recorded rather than hidden.

What Existing Standards and Formalisms Already Solve
The comparison belongs after the language proposal because otherwise SLEnglish is easily defined only by opposition. RDF, OWL, SHACL, SPARQL, PROV, Common Logic, controlled natural languages, Datalog, Answer Set Programming, constraint solvers, temporal formalisms, and workflow standards each solve substantial problems. The research question is not whether they can represent knowledge. It is whether an additional source-level language improves the passage from natural language to auditable, heterogeneous execution.
RDF provides a general graph data model and a mature ecosystem for identifiers, linked data, federation, and interchange. OWL provides description-logic semantics for classes and properties under defined profiles. SHACL validates graph shapes. SPARQL queries RDF datasets. PROV supplies a standard vocabulary for entities, activities, agents, derivation, attribution, and generation. Common Logic provides a family of first-order representations. These capabilities are baselines and targets for interoperability, not obsolete technologies to dismiss.
Controlled natural languages address a different boundary. Attempto Controlled English, Common Logic Controlled English, PENG, and related systems show that readable restricted language can map deterministically to formal structures. Their trade-offs among precision, expressiveness, naturalness, and simplicity have been studied systematically (Kuhn 2014). SLEnglish differs in degree and architecture: it sacrifices more surface naturalness, assumes LLM-assisted translation, exposes SSA identity, and uses open path-addressed operator contracts. Those differences require evidence, not rhetorical claims of novelty.
A new representation language should begin by acknowledging what existing formalisms already do well. Controlled Natural Languages provide readable entry points with explicit interpretation rules. Formal semantics offers principled accounts of quantification, discourse, events, modality, and reference. RDF provides a simple graph interchange model; RDFS and OWL support ontology semantics; SHACL validates graph shapes; SPARQL queries graphs; PROV-O represents entities, activities, agents, and derivations. Common Logic provides a first-order interchange framework. Datalog, Answer Set Programming, temporal calculi, SAT, SMT, CSP, theorem provers, and workflow systems each supply mature execution semantics for particular classes of problems.
The relevant comparison is therefore not expressive possibility in the abstract. Almost any finite structure can be encoded in JSON, RDF, relational tables, or a general programming language. The questions are engineering questions: Which representation is easiest for an LLM to generate correctly? Which keeps an n-ary event, its roles, and its provenance locally inspectable? Which permits stable semantic diffs? Which exposes a dependency graph without a separate reconstruction step? Which makes it cheap to route one claim to OWL and another to SMT while retaining common identity and source links? Which failures are visible to a reviewer rather than buried in adapters?
Traditional CNLs often preserve a substantial amount of English surface grammar. That can improve naturalness and direct authoring, but it requires a grammar sophisticated enough to regulate articles, agreement, relative clauses, quantifier scope, anaphora, and permitted verb frames. A representation that is designed primarily as an LLM compilation target can make a different trade. It can abandon subject–verb–object as its computational substrate, expose roles by name, and tolerate a more visibly formal surface. Human users review the semantics rather than pretending to write ordinary prose without ambiguity.
Formal semantic representations such as Discourse Representation Structures are richer than flat triples and can preserve discourse referents, negation, quantification, and anaphoric structure. Their breadth is valuable for interpretation research. They are not automatically ideal as a stable authoring and execution language for scientific packages. Production systems still need source identities, package versioning, module imports, operator contracts, engine routing, coverage, incremental invalidation, effect policies, and proof receipts. SLEnglish treats these engineering obligations as part of the language environment rather than as downstream infrastructure.
The most important principle inherited from the earlier survey is that the semantic pivot should not pretend to be the final logic. It should preserve identities, roles, propositions, contexts, evidence, alternatives, and dependency information sufficiently well that specialised lowerings remain possible. Some questions can be answered relationally over the pivot. Others require a temporal formula, a constraint system, a probabilistic model, a transition system, or a proof assistant. The common language coordinates these methods; it does not erase their differences.
This portfolio approach creates its own obligations. Every lowering must declare which source distinctions it preserves, approximates, rejects, or ignores. A proof in the target formalism is useful only when linked to the compilation assumptions. A contradiction produced by one engine must not be silently combined with a default conclusion from another profile. Certificates require a common envelope without forcing a common proof calculus. SLEnglish profiles are intended to make these boundaries explicit and testable.
The research claim is narrow enough to falsify. SLEnglish should be retained only if its uniform source form reduces generation errors, adapter complexity, review time, and provenance loss on target workloads. If a conventional CNL yields better fidelity and correction cost, the surface should become more natural. If RDF plus SHACL and a rule engine produces equivalent packages with less complexity, SLEnglish may remain only a source syntax or be abandoned. A serious alternative earns its place by measurable workflow properties, not by novelty of notation.
The Semantic Web stack is the strongest baseline because it separates concerns deliberately. RDF offers Web-scale identifiers and a uniform graph model. OWL provides description-logic-based ontology profiles with well-understood entailment. SHACL defines validation over RDF graphs. SPARQL provides query and update. PROV-O supplies reusable provenance concepts. JSON-LD connects graph data to familiar serialisation. These are not failed technologies. They solve interoperability problems that any new system would be foolish to ignore.
The mismatch arises from the target workflow. A scientific claim may involve an n-ary event, source attribution, evidence mode, confidence, probability, temporal validity, measurement uncertainty, a causal interpretation, a validation constraint, a derivation rule, a query, and an execution trace. In an RDF-centred implementation these concerns are normally distributed across event nodes, reification or triple terms, named graphs, shapes, ontology axioms, provenance vocabularies, rule engines, query languages, and workflow systems. The architecture is modular, but each boundary introduces identifiers, mappings, serialisations, version rules, and ownership questions.
An LLM compiler must then generate a coordinated artefact across several languages. A human reviewer must reconstruct one semantic unit from dispersed triples and metadata. A runtime must decide which layer owns negation, closure, defaults, time, conflict, and explanation. SLEnglish proposes a syntactically uniform source in which a semantic operator and all its named roles remain local to one node. It can still compile to RDF and related standards; the difference is authoring locality and circuit identity, not a claim that triples lack expressive power.
N-ary events illustrate the point. A transfer may include agent, theme, recipient, origin, destination, instrument, time, purpose, and resulting ownership. RDF represents this correctly by reifying the event as a resource and attaching role triples. SLEnglish does essentially the same semantically, but keeps the roles in one canonical node whose SSA identity already functions as a graph vertex and cache key. A reviewer can see the event as one unit. A schema can validate required roles. A circuit sees typed input ports without another graph-construction pass.
The open-world assumption of OWL is invaluable for incomplete distributed knowledge. It is not a universal policy. A scientific dataset may be closed for a declared table and revision. A compliance rule may require defaults and exceptions. A planning query may need negation as failure. A contradiction-tolerant review may need paraconsistent status. A numeric claim may require SMT rather than description-logic reasoning. The SLEnglish source must therefore name its profile and coverage rather than allowing one backend’s assumptions to become ambient.
Interoperability remains a core requirement. A class hierarchy should be exportable to OWL when it falls inside an OWL profile. Graph-shaped facts should be exportable to RDF. Validation constraints should lower to SHACL where semantics align. Provenance should map to PROV-O. Queries may compile to SPARQL, Datalog, SQL, or another declared interpreter. The compiler must document semantic loss in both directions. The project fails if it reinvents mature standards while offering no measurable advantage at the compilation and execution boundary.
The fairest experiment is package-level. Given the same natural-language research material, one team builds an RDF/OWL/SHACL/SPARQL/PROV package and another builds a SLEnglish package with equivalent lowerings. Metrics include compiler validity, human correction time, artefact count, semantic locality, source alignment, query accuracy, update impact, proof trace quality, interoperability, and false assurance. The outcome may support a hybrid in which SLEnglish is an authoring and circuit language over standard interchange formats. That would still be a successful result.
Logic-programming and solver traditions provide the operational semantics that SLEnglish itself does not attempt to replace. Datalog supports recursive, explainable closure over relations. ASP supports defaults, exceptions, alternative stable models, and optimisation. SAT, SMT, and CSP systems support bounded logical and arithmetic constraints. Temporal logics, event calculi, automata, and model checking address change and behaviour. Theorem provers address deductive proof. The relevant question is how reliably a SLEnglish fragment can be lowered to each formalism while preserving source alignment and reporting unsupported content.
Graph and ontology standards also provide governance lessons. Stable identifiers, explicit vocabularies, profile restrictions, validation languages, and federated publication are mature practices. A SLEnglish implementation should reuse them where possible. A path-addressed operator may export an RDF identity; a type hierarchy may compile to OWL; constraints may compile to SHACL; provenance may map to PROV; graph queries may compile to SPARQL. The adapter must state whether the mapping is exact, partial, approximate, or one-way.
The source-level proposal is justified only where it improves semantic locality. An n-ary event encoded as several triples is not intrinsically defective, but the author or reviewer may find it easier to inspect one canonical statement containing named roles. A path-based contract can keep schema, tests, rendering, and lowering near the operator definition. SSA identities can support diffing and dependency analysis before graph expansion. These are engineering hypotheses about authoring and maintenance, not claims that graph representation is incapable of expressing the content.
Existing approach
Capability that SLEnglish should reuse or match
RDF and linked data
Stable identifiers, graph interchange, federation, established serialisations, and a broad tooling ecosystem.
OWL and description logics
Formal class and property semantics with decidable profiles and mature reasoners.
SHACL
Declarative validation of graph shapes, cardinalities, and constraints.
SPARQL
Standard graph query, federation, filtering, aggregation, and update mechanisms.
PROV
Interoperable provenance for entities, activities, agents, use, generation, derivation, and attribution.
Common Logic
A standard framework for exchange among first-order logic dialects.
Controlled natural languages
Deterministic mappings from constrained readable input to formal semantics.
Datalog and ASP
Rule evaluation, recursion, defaults, exceptions, model generation, and explainability.
SMT, CSP, SAT, and model checking
Efficient decision procedures, witnesses, unsatisfiable cores, and bounded verification.
Workflow and research-object standards
Execution metadata, packaging, environments, artefact lineage, and reproducibility.

claims.statement: The application to science begins with a problem that rerunnable code does not settle. A result can be reproduced while its relationship to a prose claim remains implicit. The book proposes recording the semantic dependencies connecting evidence, assumptions, methods, and conclusions. A corrected dataset can then identify which dependent claims require renewed attention. Affected does not automatically mean false, and the book preserves that distinction. A reviewer can challenge a particular dependency instead of rejecting an entire narrative. The chapter develops this semantic build system as a companion to scientific explanation.

From Reproducible Computation to an Executable Argument
Executable science is the broader application that motivates the language, but the phrase must remain narrower than the claim that science can be reduced to software. Scientific work includes concept formation, measurement, modelling, interpretation, criticism, ethical judgement, institutional authority, and revision. The proposed change is that a larger share of the operational and evidential structure should become inspectable and queryable, while unresolved judgement remains explicit rather than being simulated as deterministic output.
The semantic build-system analogy is useful because scientific claims depend on artefacts and assumptions in ways that ordinary documents record only partially. A build system knows which outputs depend on which inputs and what must be recomputed after change. An executable research object should similarly know which conclusions depend on a dataset revision, a calibration, an identity rule, a causal interpretation, a software environment, a reported source, or a reviewer-approved exception. The analogy does not imply that every dependency is mechanical; it requires each dependency to state its kind.
Executable science is often reduced to reproducible code. Reproducible computation is indispensable, but it does not make a scientific argument executable. A notebook can rerun a regression while leaving unclear which sentence the regression supports, which assumptions are required, which uncertainty is statistical rather than structural, which dataset revision was used, and which claims depend on a contested interpretation of identity or causation. The gap is not execution of the calculation; it is execution of the argument’s semantic dependencies.
A scientific project can be treated as a semantic build system. Concepts, hypotheses, protocols, instruments, observations, datasets, transformations, models, simulations, results, claims, critiques, and conclusions become typed nodes connected to source material and executable artefacts. A build resolves definitions, checks units and scopes, validates protocol obligations, executes analyses, derives eligible claims, reports contradictions, and materialises proof and provenance graphs. The prose remains a human view over that build rather than being replaced by it.
SLEnglish files do not duplicate datasets, code, or workflow specifications. They state the relations among them. A measurement node identifies the variable, entity, unit, uncertainty, instrument, calibration, source field, and time. An analysis node identifies code, environment, inputs, method, parameters, and output. A claim node states which results support it, under which assumptions, population, temporal scope, identity criteria, and causal mode. A review node can challenge one premise without rewriting the original claim.
Claims become build targets. A conclusion depends on observations, statistical analyses, simulations, background theory, methodological assumptions, and interpretive choices. Some dependencies are deductive; some probabilistic; some defeasible; some institutional. The objective is not to force them into one proof calculus. It is to type the dependency and preserve the provenance so that changes propagate appropriately.
When a dataset is corrected, a software dependency changes, a source is retracted, or an ontology is revised, the build graph identifies affected downstream claims. Some conclusions may remain textually identical while their support weakens. Others may need recomputation. Superseded results remain in prior epochs. This is the semantic analogue of incremental compilation and gives scientific revision a more precise memory.
Research objects, FAIR workflows, notebooks, RO-Crate, provenance standards, containers, and workflow languages already solve important parts of this problem. They package data, code, environments, runs, and metadata. SLEnglish targets the missing semantic layer of the prose claim and its relation to those artefacts. It should interoperate with mature tooling rather than replace it.
Executable science should not be confused with fully automated science. A machine may establish that a conclusion follows from declared assumptions while experts dispute the assumptions, measurement validity, causal interpretation, or social relevance. Formalisation localises that disagreement; it does not eliminate judgement. The system’s success lies partly in making disputes addressable at the node where they arise.
The strongest near-term use cases are bounded: verifying that reported numbers match outputs; checking unit and population consistency; linking claims to exact source spans and analysis runs; exposing unsupported causal language; tracking retractions; validating protocol conditions; comparing theory versions; and asking structured questions across a research package. These tasks can demonstrate value without claiming machine understanding of all science.
A paper in this architecture has two aligned surfaces. The first is ordinary prose, which preserves rhetoric, explanation, uncertainty, and disciplinary style. The second is an executable semantic package containing the claims selected for formal treatment. Alignment may be paragraph-level, sentence-level, or span-level depending on importance. Readers can stay in prose until they need to inspect evidence, query a claim, compare versions, or reproduce a derivation.
The package begins with a concept layer. Terms are defined, mapped to external vocabularies where useful, and versioned. Identity criteria are explicit for samples, organisms, datasets, models, software versions, institutions, and populations. Units, scales, temporal frames, and missing-value semantics are declared. Competing definitions can coexist in namespaces rather than being collapsed into a supposedly neutral ontology.
The hypothesis layer distinguishes conjecture, operational hypothesis, statistical hypothesis, mechanistic model, and prediction. A hypothesis specifies conditions under which it would be challenged, but executable science should not reduce scientific status to one falsification operator. Replication, calibration, exploratory analysis, model comparison, severe testing, Bayesian updating, and qualitative evidence require different profiles. The semantic package makes the test relation visible rather than imposing one philosophy of science.
The protocol layer connects planned actions to actual execution. Preconditions, interventions, measurement schedules, randomisation, blinding, inclusion criteria, exclusions, stopping rules, and deviations can be represented. External workflow engines and laboratory systems remain operational authorities. SLEnglish records the semantic contract and imports receipts. A protocol query can identify which conclusions rely on a deviation or unavailable measurement.
The result layer distinguishes raw observation, processed measurement, statistical estimate, model output, simulation result, and derived quantity. Probability is separated from confidence in the estimate. Statistical uncertainty is separated from structural, measurement, and model uncertainty. Bounds and units are mandatory under scientific profiles. A result without source and method remains a proposition but cannot be promoted to an empirical claim.
The claim layer records modality and scope. An association is not a causal effect. A population average is not an individual prediction. A result inside a simulation is not an observation in the actual world. A bounded verification is not an unbounded theorem. A claim states which transformation licensed it and which assumptions remain external. The renderer uses these distinctions to prevent familiar overstatements.
The discussion layer can represent competing interpretations rather than only the authors’ preferred narrative. A reviewer may accept data and analysis while rejecting an identity criterion or causal layer. An alternative model can share evidence but derive different implications. May/must analysis can show which conclusions are robust across the admissible interpretations. The paper becomes capable of exposing its own hinge assumptions.
The publication artefact records a build lock: source digests, library versions, compiler, model profile, engine versions, environment, policies, and reviewer decisions. This does not guarantee that the science is correct. It makes the machine-mediated transformations inspectable and the computational parts replayable. The reproducible unit becomes the argument package, not only the notebook.
SLEnglish contributes a human-facing representation for this semantic layer. Existing workflow and research-object standards remain responsible for packaging files, data, code, environments, and runs. Domain repositories remain responsible for authoritative records. Formal systems remain responsible for their own proofs or certificates. SLEnglish links these artefacts to propositions, contexts, evidence, interpretations, and queries so that the relation between a calculation and a published claim does not remain an informal caption.
The build graph should distinguish normative from descriptive dependencies. A protocol may require an action without establishing that it occurred. A dataset may contain an observation without licensing a causal conclusion. A reviewer may authorise publication without endorsing every interpretation. A legal permission may allow data use without establishing scientific validity. The common representation is valuable only if these different relations remain typed.
Scientific change is then represented as revision rather than overwrite. A corrected dataset, altered calibration, retracted source, changed code dependency, or new identity criterion creates a new epoch. The system identifies potentially affected claims, but it does not declare all of them false. Some require recomputation, some require reinterpretation, some retain support through independent evidence, and some become unsupported. This distinction is more faithful than treating a scientific article as either permanently valid or globally retracted.
The minimal useful outcome is not an autonomous research system. It is a document whose selected claims can answer bounded questions about source, scope, support, contradiction, dependence, and change. A reader should be able to ask which measurements support a conclusion, which assumptions are external, what would change under a competing identity model, which claims rely on a retracted source, and which parts of the argument cannot yet be represented.
